stages.topic: Passive Income vs Active Income: The Difference, with Examples
stages.brief:
Brief: Passive Income vs Active Income

**Chosen query:** passive income vs active income
**Focus keyphrase:** passive income vs active income. Use it in the title, the intro and one or two more times. Don't use it in headings.
**Working title:** Passive Income vs Active Income: The Difference, With Examples (and What the IRS Actually Calls "Passive")
**Search intent:** A definition plus a comparison, with examples. The current top results are SoFi, US News, SmartAsset, Edvisors, a few investment and real-estate firm blogs, and one CPA firm. Almost all of them give a short definition ("money you earn without active participation"), a list of examples, pros and cons, and one line about taxes.

**Where current results fall short, and what we add:**
1. **They treat two meanings as one.** Everyday "passive income" means money that keeps coming in after the work is done. The IRS uses "passive activity" in a much narrower sense. Under IRS rules, dividends and interest are *portfolio* income, not passive income. Income from a book or design you made yourself is not passive activity income either. Rentals are generally passive even if you work hard on them. No ranking page lays this out clearly for online earners.
2. **The online-earner case is missing.** Royalties from your own ebook, digital downloads and product shops are usually business income. That means Schedule C and self-employment tax. Readers who call these "passive" are often surprised.
3. **A decision table.** For each common example: active or passive in everyday terms, what the IRS calls it, what the platform takes (sourced), and the ongoing work that makes it less passive than it sounds.
4. **A scam check.** The FTC has taken action against companies selling "passive income" systems. These cases make the "nothing is fully passive" point with official evidence rather than opinion.

Tone: US tax framing, flagged as general information, not tax advice. Readers outside the US should check their own rules. Never promise income.

---

## Outline

**Intro (2–3 short paragraphs).** Active income is paid for work as you do it. Passive income keeps arriving after the setup work, but almost nothing is truly hands-off. There's also a second, legal meaning of "passive" that matters at tax time. This article covers both, with examples.

### H2: The quick difference
- Plain definitions, written in our own words. Don't quote competitor pages.
- Active: wages, freelance fees, commissions. You stop working, the pay stops.
- Passive (everyday meaning): money from something you built or bought earlier, such as a book, a digital product, a dividend-paying investment or a rental.
- A short note that "passive" describes how the money arrives, not how much work it took.

### H2: Examples side by side (the decision table)
Columns: Example | Everyday label | How the IRS generally classifies it | Platform cut or fees (sourced) | Ongoing work.

| Example | Everyday label | IRS treatment (general) | Platform cut / fees | Ongoing work |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Salary/wages | Active | Personal service income, not passive [F5] | — | Ongoing |
| Freelance client work | Active | Self-employment income; SE tax if net earnings are $400 or more [F5, F8, F9] | Depends on platform. Don't state figures; link internally | Ongoing |
| Self-published ebook (KDP) | "Passive" | Self-employed writer: Schedule C, not Schedule E [F11]. Not passive activity income if your efforts significantly contributed to creating it [F6] | 35% or 70% royalty options; conditions apply [F13–F15] | Marketing, updates, price changes |
| Digital downloads on Etsy | "Passive" | Business income if you run it as a business (Schedule C/SE logic) [F8, F9] | Possible one-time set-up fee, $0.20 listing fee, listings expire after 4 months, 6.5% transaction fee, plus payment processing [F16–F19] | Renewals, customer messages, new listings |
| Dividends/interest | Passive | **Portfolio** income, not passive activity income [F4]. May face the 3.8% NIIT above set thresholds [F10] | Brokerage fees vary; don't state any | Low |
| Rental property | Passive | Generally a passive activity even with material participation, unless you're a real estate professional [F1, F7] | — | Often substantial (tenants, repairs) |
| Owning part of a business you don't work in | Passive | Passive if you don't materially participate [F1] | — | Low |

Writer: the "IRS treatment" column must stay general ("generally", "usually"). Add a line saying individual situations vary and a tax professional can confirm.

### H2: What "passive" means at tax time (US)
- H3: **The IRS has only two kinds of passive activity** [F1]. Quote that wording.
- H3: **Material participation: the hour tests.** Summarize the seven tests: more than 500 hours; substantially all the participation; more than 100 hours and at least as much as anyone else; and so on [F2]. Add "any work you do in connection with an activity in which you own an interest is treated as participation" [F3].
- H3: **Portfolio income is a separate bucket.** Interest, dividends, annuities, and royalties not earned in the ordinary course of a trade or business [F4].
- H3: **Why the label matters.** The passive activity rules mainly limit deducting *losses* (Pub 925 scope) [F0]. The 3.8% NIIT applies to passive-activity business income and investment income above set thresholds, but not to wages or income from an active business [F10]. Active self-employment income carries self-employment tax: 12.4% Social Security plus 2.9% Medicare, on 92.35% of net earnings, usually when net earnings are $400 or more [F8, F9].
- Don't claim passive income is "taxed at lower rates". Pub 925 doesn't say that, and qualified dividend and capital gains rates weren't sourced here.

### H2: Why most online "passive income" is really a business
- Your own ebook, course, templates or designs: if your personal efforts significantly contributed to creating the property, the income is excluded from passive activity income [F6]. Self-employed writers and artists report royalties on Schedule C [F11]. Schedule C income is generally subject to SE tax [F8].
- Platforms keep charging as long as the product stays live: Etsy listings expire after four months, and auto-renew charges $0.20 each time [F17, F18]. KDP's 70% option deducts delivery costs and only applies to buyers in certain territories [F14, F15].
- Upkeep that makes it less passive: customer questions, updates, renewals, marketing. Keep these as general statements, no numbers.

### H2: How long before it earns, and what it costs to set up
- Don't give timelines or income figures; there's no source for either. Frame it as what to check before starting: upfront costs (set-up and listing fees [F16, F17]), the platform's cut [F13, F19], the time to build the asset, and whether income stops if you stop maintaining it.
- Optional checklist: "Is it passive? Five questions." All questions should be our own framing, not facts.

### H2: Red flags in "passive income" pitches
- FTC Click Profit case (complaint allegations only, written as "the FTC alleged"): promised "passive income" from AI-powered online stores; management fee of at least $45,000; most consumers allegedly lost their entire payments; Amazon allegedly blocked, suspended or terminated about 95% of the stores [F20–F23]. Include the FTC's own note that a complaint isn't a ruling [F24].
- FTC Publishing.com settlement: $1.5M; marketed as a "foolproof, passive income system"; course up to $1,995; most buyers allegedly never reached the promised income [F25–F27].
- Takeaway list, our own framing: guaranteed income, big upfront fees, testimonials you can't verify, "done-for-you" stores.

### H2: Building a mix of active and passive income
- Our own framing: active income pays the bills while a slower asset is built. Keep it short, with no income promises. Link internal articles here.

### H2: FAQ (3–4 short questions)
- Is freelancing passive income? (No: active, SE tax [F5, F8].)
- Are dividends passive income? (Everyday meaning yes; IRS calls them portfolio income [F4].)
- Is rental income passive? (Generally yes under IRS rules, even with material participation, unless you're a real estate professional [F7].)
- Is ebook income passive? (It may feel passive, but for a self-employed writer it's Schedule C [F11] and excluded from passive activity income [F6].)

## Product link
None. There's no product for this pillar, and none would be justified at any step.

## SOURCE NOTES

**S1. IRS Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules.** https://www.irs.gov/publications/p925. The page states the tax year "2025"; there's no publish date on the page.
- **F0 (scope):** "This publication discusses two sets of rules that may limit the amount of your deductible loss from a trade, business, rental, or other income-producing activity. The first part of the publication discusses the passive activity rules."
- **F1:** "There are two kinds of passive activities. Trade or business activities in which you don't materially participate during the year. Rental activities, even if you do materially participate in them, unless you're a real estate professional."
- **F2:** "A trade or business activity isn't a passive activity if you materially participated in the activity. You materially participated in a trade or business activity for a tax year if you satisfy any of the following tests." The tests:
  - "You participated in the activity for more than 500 hours."
  - "Your participation was substantially all the participation in the activity of all individuals for the tax year, including the participation of individuals who didn't own any interest in the activity."
  - "You participated in the activity for more than 100 hours during the tax year, and you participated at least as much as any other individual (including individuals who didn't own any interest in the activity) for the year."
  - The significant-participation test: more than 500 hours combined across activities of more than 100 hours each.
  - Material participation "for any 5 (whether or not consecutive) of the 10 immediately preceding tax years."
  - The personal service activity test. The excerpt didn't show its wording; mention it only as "other tests".
  - "Based on all the facts and circumstances, you participated in the activity on a regular, continuous, and substantial basis during the year." Condition attached: "You didn't materially participate in the activity under test (7) if you participated in the activity for 100 hours or less during the year."
- **F3:** "In general, any work you do in connection with an activity in which you own an interest is treated as participation in the activity."
- **F4:** "Passive activity income doesn't include the following items… Portfolio income. This includes interest, dividends, annuities, and royalties not derived in the ordinary course of a trade or business. It includes gain or loss from the disposition of property that produces these types of income or that is held for investment."
- **F5:** "Personal service income. This includes salaries, wages, commissions, self-employment income from trade or business activities in which you materially participated, deferred compensation, taxable social security and other retirement benefits…"
- **F6:** Also excluded from passive activity income: "Any income from intangible property, such as a patent, copyright, or literary, musical, or artistic composition, if your personal efforts significantly contributed to the creation of the property."
- **F7:** "Generally, rental activities are passive activities even if you materially participated in them. However, if you qualified as a real estate professional, rental real estate activities in which you materially participated aren't passive activities."

**S2. IRS Topic no. 554, Self-employment tax.** https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc554. No date on the page.
- **F8:** "You usually must pay self-employment tax if you had net earnings from self-employment of $400 or more. Generally, the amount subject to self-employment tax is 92.35% of your net earnings from self-employment. You calculate net earnings by subtracting ordinary and necessary trade or business expenses from the gross income you derived from your trade or business." Who counts: "a sole proprietor (including an independent contractor), a partner in a partnership… or are otherwise in business for yourself."
- **F9:** "This rate consists of 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare taxes." Conditions: "The law sets a maximum amount of net earnings subject to the Social Security tax. This amount changes annually. All of your net earnings are subject to the Medicare tax." Also: "you can deduct one-half of the self-employment tax."

**S3. IRS Topic no. 559, Net investment income tax.** https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc559. No date on the page; it references the 2025 threshold for trusts.
- **F10:** "A 3.8 percent net investment income tax (NIIT) applies to individuals, estates, and trusts that have net investment income above applicable threshold amounts." For individuals, it applies to the lesser of net investment income or the MAGI excess over "$250,000 for married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse; $125,000 for married filing separately; $200,000 for single or head of household." NII includes "interest, dividends, certain annuities, royalties, and rents (unless derived in a trade or business in which the NIIT doesn't apply)" and "income derived in a trade or business which is a passive activity…" Exclusion: "The NIIT doesn't apply to wages, unemployment compensation, or income from an active business."

**S4. IRS 2025 Instructions for Schedule E (Form 1040).** https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1040se. Covers tax year 2025.
- **F11:** "If you are in business as a self-employed writer, inventor, artist, etc., report your royalty income and expenses on Schedule C, not on Schedule E."
- **F12:** "Use Schedule E (Form 1040) to report income or loss from rental real estate, royalties, partnerships, S corporations, estates, trusts, and residual interests in REMICs." Also: "If you received $10 or more in royalties during 2025, the payer should send you a Form 1099-MISC or similar statement by January 31, 2026."

**S5. Amazon KDP Help, "eBook Royalties".** https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G200644210. No date on the page.
- **F13:** "You can choose between two royalty options for each of your eBooks: the 35% royalty option and the 70% royalty option." "If you select the 35% royalty option, your royalty will be 35% of your list price without VAT for each unit sold."
- **F14:** "If you select the 70% royalty option, your royalty will be 70% of your list price without VAT, less delivery costs (average delivery costs are $0.06 per unit sold, and vary by file size), for each eligible book sold to customers in the 70% territories, and 35% of the list price without VAT for each unit sold to customers residing outside the 70% territories."
- **F15:** "The 70% royalty option is for in-copyright works only. Works in the public domain or consisting primarily of public domain content are only eligible for the 35% royalty option."
- The 70% option has list-price requirements on the KDP Pricing Page, which wasn't read for this brief. Don't state price ranges.

**S6. Etsy, Fees & Payments Policy.** https://www.etsy.com/legal/fees/. The page says "Last updated on Oct 5, 2026".
- **F16:** "To open your Etsy shop, you may be required to pay a one-time set-up fee. Please note that if applicable, the set-up fee will be displayed and charged as part of the shop set-up process." No amount is given in this excerpt, so don't state one. Also: "all service fees, including prepaid fees, are non-refundable."
- **F17:** "You will be charged a listing fee of $0.20 USD for each item that you list for sale on Etsy.com or Etsy's mobile apps." The fee applies "whether or not the listed item sells, unless you create a private listing." "Etsy.com listings expire after four months."
- **F18:** "Etsy's automatic renewals feature will automatically renew your listings at the end of the four-month listing period… You will be charged the listing fee of $0.20 for each of these listings until you cancel automatic renewals."
- **F19:** "When you make a sale through Etsy.com, you will be charged a transaction fee of 6.5% of the price you display for each listing plus the amount you charge for shipping and gift wrapping." Payment processing fees for Etsy Payments are charged separately. The rate varies by country and wasn't captured, so say only "plus payment processing fees".

**S7. FTC press release, "FTC Acts to Stop 'Click Profit' Online Business Opportunity that Has Cost Consumers At Least $14 Million".** Dated March 18, 2025 (modified July 30, 2025). https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/03/ftc-acts-stop-click-profit-online-business-opportunity-has-cost-consumers-least-14-million. Read via web_fetch because read_source returned a 404.
- **F20:** "the FTC alleged that Click Profit and its owners deceived consumers by promising they could make large sums in "passive income" using a proprietary system powered by artificial intelligence."
- **F21:** "Consumers who purchased the company's business opportunity were charged a "management fee" of at least $45,000, in addition to thousands of dollars more, purportedly to buy inventory for their stores."
- **F22:** "most consumers lose their entire payments, and some are saddled with burdensome credit card debt and unsold products." These are allegations, so write "the complaint alleges".
- **F23:** "According to the complaint, Amazon has blocked, suspended, or terminated about 95% of Click Profit's stores."
- **F24 (required caveat):** "The Commission files a complaint when it has "reason to believe" that the named defendants are violating or are about to violate the law… The case will be decided by the court."

**S8. FTC press release, "Publishing.com to Pay $1.5 Million for Misleading Consumers about How Much Income They Could Earn…".** Dated April 13, 2026 (modified July 2, 2026). https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/04/publishingcom-pay-15-million-misleading-consumers-about-how-much-income-they-could-earn-using. Read via web_fetch.
- **F25:** "Publishing.com LLC and its two principals will pay $1.5 million and be required to substantiate earnings claims in the future to settle Federal Trade Commission charges…"
- **F26:** "AIA is Publishing.com's self-publishing course, which can cost up to $1,995… the company used free online videos to entice consumers to purchase what it describes as a foolproof, passive income system."
- **F27:** "Most consumers who bought Publishing.com's products and services, however, never achieved the income the company promised in its advertising, according to the FTC's complaint." Condition: this is a proposed consent order, subject to 30 days of public comment before the Commission decides whether to make it final. Write "agreed to pay … to settle FTC charges"; don't say "was found guilty".

**Writer guardrails**
- Every number in the article must come from F0–F27 and link to its source in the same paragraph.
- Don't give income figures, timelines to first earnings, or claims that passive income is taxed at lower rates.
- Present tax content as general US information, not advice.

article.title: Passive Income vs Active Income: The Difference, With Examples (and What the IRS Actually Calls "Passive")
article.seo_title: Passive Income vs Active Income: Examples and IRS Rules
article.meta_description: Passive income vs active income explained with examples, a side-by-side table, how the IRS defines passive activity, and red flags in passive income pitches.
article.excerpt: Active income stops when you stop working. Passive income keeps arriving after the setup. But the IRS uses "passive" in a much narrower sense, and most online income counts as a business. Here are the examples, the tax labels and the red flags.
article.content_html:
The simplest way to frame passive income vs active income is this. Active income is paid for work as you do it. Passive income keeps arriving after the setup work is done. In practice, almost nothing that earns money is completely hands-off. Books need marketing, shops need listings renewed, and rentals need tenants and repairs.

There is also a second meaning of "passive" that matters at tax time. In the US, the IRS uses "passive activity" in a much narrower sense than everyday speech does. Some things people casually call passive income, such as dividends or royalties from a book you wrote yourself, fall outside the IRS definition. This guide covers both meanings, with examples side by side.

The tax notes here are general US information, not tax advice. If you live outside the US, check your own country's rules. For your own situation, a tax professional can confirm how your income is classified.

The quick difference

  • Active income is money paid in exchange for work you are doing now. Examples include a salary or hourly wages, freelance fees and sales commissions. If you stop working, the pay stops.
  • Passive income, in the everyday sense, is money from something you built or bought earlier. Examples include a self-published book, a digital download, dividend-paying investments or a rental property. Each payment doesn't depend on you putting in another hour that day.

"Passive" describes how the money arrives, not how much work it took. An ebook or a set of design templates can take months to create. That work is simply done up front instead of being billed by the hour, and most of these assets still need some upkeep afterward.

Examples side by side

The table below puts common income streams next to each other. It shows the everyday label, how the IRS generally treats each one, what the platform takes where a source is available, and the ongoing work that makes it less passive than it sounds.

ExampleEveryday labelHow the IRS generally classifies itPlatform cut or feesOngoing work
Salary or wagesActivePersonal service income, which IRS Publication 925 lists as not passive activity incomeNoneOngoing: you work, you get paid
Freelance client workActiveSelf-employment income. You usually owe self-employment tax if net earnings from self-employment are $400 or more (IRS Topic 554)Depends on the platform. See what each platform takesOngoing: finding clients, delivering work
Self-published ebook (Amazon KDP)"Passive"If you are in business as a self-employed writer, royalties go on Schedule C, not Schedule E (Schedule E instructions). Income from a literary work is excluded from passive activity income if your personal efforts significantly contributed to creating it (Pub 925)You choose a 35% or 70% royalty option. The 70% option deducts delivery costs and applies only to eligible sales in certain territories (KDP eBook Royalties)Marketing, updates, price changes
Digital downloads on Etsy"Passive"Usually business income if you run it as a business, so the self-employment rules generally apply (IRS Topic 554)A possible one-time set-up fee, a $0.20 listing fee, listings that expire after four months, a 6.5% transaction fee, plus payment processing fees (Etsy Fees & Payments Policy)Renewals, customer messages, new listings
Dividends and interestPassivePortfolio income, not passive activity income (Pub 925). It may be subject to the 3.8% net investment income tax above set income thresholds (IRS Topic 559)Brokerage fees varyLow
Rental propertyPassiveGenerally a passive activity even if you materially participate, unless you qualify as a real estate professional (Pub 925)NoneOften substantial: tenants, repairs, vacancies
Owning part of a business you don't work inPassiveA passive activity if you don't materially participate during the year (Pub 925)NoneLow

The IRS column is a general summary. Individual situations vary, and the details depend on facts the table can't capture, such as how many hours you put in and whether you are in business. A tax professional can confirm how your own income is treated.

What "passive" means at tax time (US)

The IRS recognizes only two kinds of passive activity

According to IRS Publication 925, "There are two kinds of passive activities":

  • "Trade or business activities in which you don't materially participate during the year."
  • "Rental activities, even if you do materially participate in them, unless you're a real estate professional."

That is a much narrower idea than the everyday "money while you sleep." Under these rules, a business is only passive for you if you don't materially participate in it, however automated it may be.

Material participation: the hour tests

Pub 925 says a trade or business activity isn't a passive activity if you materially participated in it. You materially participated for a tax year if you meet any one of several tests. They include these (IRS Publication 925):

  • You participated in the activity for more than 500 hours.
  • Your participation was substantially all the participation in the activity by all individuals for the year, including people who didn't own an interest in it.
  • You participated for more than 100 hours during the year, and at least as much as any other individual, including non-owners.
  • A significant-participation test: more than 500 hours combined across activities in which you participated for more than 100 hours each.
  • You materially participated in the activity for any 5 of the 10 immediately preceding tax years, whether or not those years were consecutive.
  • Based on all the facts and circumstances, you participated on a regular, continuous and substantial basis during the year. You can't meet this test if you participated for 100 hours or less.

There are other tests too, so read Pub 925 for the full list. It also says: "In general, any work you do in connection with an activity in which you own an interest is treated as participation in the activity." For a solo online business, where you do nearly all the work yourself, that matters a lot.

Portfolio income is a separate bucket

Pub 925 says passive activity income doesn't include portfolio income. That covers "interest, dividends, annuities, and royalties not derived in the ordinary course of a trade or business," plus gain or loss from selling property that produces that kind of income or is held for investment (IRS Publication 925). So the dividends people often hold up as the classic example of passive income are, in IRS terms, portfolio income.

Royalties can land in different places depending on your situation. Schedule E is used to report income from rental real estate and royalties, among other things. However, the instructions say self-employed writers, inventors and artists report royalty income on Schedule C instead. They also note that if you received $10 or more in royalties during 2025, the payer should send you a Form 1099-MISC or similar statement by January 31, 2026 (IRS 2025 Instructions for Schedule E).

Why the label matters

  • Losses. Pub 925 describes the passive activity rules as rules that "may limit the amount of your deductible loss" from a trade, business, rental or other income-producing activity (IRS Publication 925). The label mainly matters for how losses can be deducted.
  • Net investment income tax. A 3.8% net investment income tax (NIIT) applies to individuals, estates and trusts with net investment income above set thresholds. For individuals, those thresholds are based on modified adjusted gross income: $200,000 for single or head of household, $250,000 for married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse, and $125,000 for married filing separately. Net investment income includes interest, dividends, certain annuities, royalties and rents (with exceptions), and income from a trade or business that is a passive activity. The IRS says the NIIT doesn't apply to wages, unemployment compensation or income from an active business (IRS Topic 559).
  • Self-employment tax. Active self-employment income works differently. You usually must pay self-employment tax if net earnings from self-employment are $400 or more. Generally, 92.35% of those net earnings is subject to the tax. The rate is made up of 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare. There is an annual cap on earnings subject to the Social Security part, and you can deduct one-half of the self-employment tax (IRS Topic 554).

For most online earners, the practical point in the passive income vs active income question is this: calling income "passive" in conversation doesn't change how the IRS treats it.

Why most online "passive income" is really a business

Ebooks, courses, templates, printables and designs are the usual examples of online passive income. In IRS terms, they rarely fit the narrow definition.

  • You made it, so it isn't passive activity income. Pub 925 excludes from passive activity income "any income from intangible property, such as a patent, copyright, or literary, musical, or artistic composition, if your personal efforts significantly contributed to the creation of the property" (IRS Publication 925).
  • Self-employed creators use Schedule C. The Schedule E instructions tell self-employed writers, inventors and artists to report royalty income and expenses on Schedule C, not Schedule E (IRS Schedule E instructions).
  • Self-employment tax usually follows. If you are a sole proprietor or otherwise in business for yourself, you usually owe self-employment tax once net earnings reach $400 (IRS Topic 554).

Platforms also keep charging for as long as your product stays live. On Etsy, listings expire after four months. If automatic renewals are on, you are charged the $0.20 listing fee for each renewed listing until you cancel them (Etsy Fees & Payments Policy). On Amazon KDP, the 70% royalty option is calculated after delivery costs, which average $0.06 per unit and vary by file size. It applies only to eligible books sold to customers in the 70% territories, and sales outside those territories earn 35% (KDP eBook Royalties). KDP also says works in the public domain, or consisting mainly of public domain content, are only eligible for the 35% option.

Then there is the upkeep that rarely appears in a passive income pitch:

  • Answering customer questions and handling refund requests
  • Updating products when tools, platforms or information change
  • Renewing listings and adjusting prices
  • Ongoing marketing, because new buyers have to find the product somehow

Our guides to print on demand for beginners and making money on Pinterest go through this upkeep for those specific models. Creator payouts are often described as passive too. To see how those payouts actually work, read about how YouTube pays creators and the TikTok Creator Rewards Program.

What it costs to set up, and what to check before you start

No reliable figure exists for how long a digital product or creator channel takes to earn money, or how much it will earn. Results vary too widely. You can, however, check the known costs and conditions before you commit:

  • Upfront fees. Etsy says you may have to pay a one-time set-up fee to open a shop, shown during set-up. It charges $0.20 per listing whether or not the item sells, unless the listing is private. Etsy also states that all service fees, including prepaid fees, are non-refundable (Etsy Fees & Payments Policy).
  • The platform's cut. Etsy charges a 6.5% transaction fee on the displayed price plus shipping and gift wrapping, with payment processing fees charged separately (Etsy). KDP pays 35% of the list price without VAT under its 35% option, or the 70% option subject to its conditions (KDP).
  • Your build time. Count the hours it will take to create the asset, and treat them as real work, because they are.
  • What happens if you stop. Find out whether income continues if you stop renewing, updating or promoting the product.

Is it passive? Five questions to ask

  1. If I stopped working on this for three months, would the income continue, shrink or stop?
  2. Does the platform charge recurring fees just to keep my product visible?
  3. Who answers customers, and how often will that be me?
  4. Did I create this myself, which may make it business income rather than passive activity income for tax purposes?
  5. Am I paying someone else a large sum up front to make it "passive" for me?

These questions are a framework for thinking, not tax tests. The IRS tests are the material participation rules described above.

Red flags in "passive income" pitches

The phrase "passive income" shows up in some deceptive business-opportunity marketing, and the Federal Trade Commission has acted against companies using it.

Click Profit. In March 2025, the FTC announced action against Click Profit, in a press release titled as an online business opportunity that "has cost consumers at least $14 million." The FTC alleged that Click Profit and its owners promised consumers they could make large sums in "passive income" using a proprietary system powered by artificial intelligence. The complaint alleges that buyers were charged a "management fee" of at least $45,000, plus thousands of dollars more, supposedly for store inventory. It also alleges that most consumers lose their entire payments, and that Amazon blocked, suspended or terminated about 95% of Click Profit's stores. The FTC notes that it files a complaint when it has "reason to believe" the law is being or is about to be violated, and that the case will be decided by the court (FTC press release on Click Profit).

Publishing.com. Publishing.com LLC and its two principals agreed to pay $1.5 million, and to substantiate future earnings claims, to settle FTC charges. According to the FTC, the company's self-publishing course could cost up to $1,995 and was marketed as a "foolproof, passive income system." The FTC's complaint says most buyers never achieved the income promised in the advertising. The settlement is a proposed consent order, open to public comment before the Commission decides whether to make it final (FTC press release on Publishing.com).

Warning signs worth taking seriously:

  • Promises of certain or effortless income
  • Large upfront fees, especially "management" or "coaching" fees in the thousands
  • Success stories and screenshots you can't verify
  • "Done-for-you" stores or systems that claim to need no work from you
  • Pressure to buy quickly, or to pay with credit you can't afford to lose

For a realistic look at what online earning involves, see whether $100 a day online is realistic.

Building a mix of active and passive income

For most people starting out, the answer isn't to choose one over the other. Active income, such as a job or freelance work, pays the bills while you slowly build an asset on the side. That asset might be a book, a template shop or a content channel. As it grows, it may cover more of your income, though nothing guarantees that it will.

A few practical points:

  • Keep your active income steady while you build. Assets usually take time, and how long is unpredictable.
  • Track the hours you spend on the "passive" side. They tell you whether it's really passive, and the IRS participation tests count hours too.
  • Set aside money for taxes on both streams. Freelance and self-published income are usually self-employment income.

If you are still choosing where to start, our overview of five ways to make money online and what each platform takes compares the main options.

FAQ

Is freelancing passive income?

No. Freelancing is active income: you are paid for work as you do it. The IRS treats self-employment income from a business you materially participate in as personal service income, not passive activity income (Pub 925). You usually owe self-employment tax if your net earnings are $400 or more (IRS Topic 554).

Are dividends passive income?

In everyday terms, yes. For tax purposes, the IRS classifies interest and dividends as portfolio income, which is not passive activity income (Pub 925).

Is rental income passive?

Generally, yes. Under IRS rules, rental activities are passive even if you materially participate in them. If you qualify as a real estate professional, rental real estate activities in which you materially participate aren't passive (Pub 925).

Is ebook income passive?

It may feel passive once the book is out, but the tax treatment usually says otherwise. If you are in business as a self-employed writer, you report royalties on Schedule C (Schedule E instructions). Income from a work you substantially created yourself is excluded from passive activity income (Pub 925).
